CausalChain: Tumor Cells -> Secretion of EVs enriched in miR-21, miR-155, and cytokine modulators (IL-6, GM-CSF) -> Uptake by mature myeloid cells (enhanced by cytokine milieu) -> Downregulation of IRF-8 and C/EBPα -> Skewed differentiation toward immunosuppressive MDSCs -> Enhanced T cell inhibition and tumor immune escape
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that tumor-derived EVs simultaneously deliver a specific cocktail of oncogenic miRNAs (miR-21 and miR-155) and critical cytokine modulators (e.g., IL-6, GM-CSF) to mature myeloid cells in the tumor microenvironment. This dual delivery mechanism leads to the downregulation of key transcription factors IRF-8 and C/EBPα which are essential for normal myeloid differentiation. As a consequence, the differentiation pathway is shifted toward the formation of immunosuppressive myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs), thereby promoting tumor immune escape. To rigorously interrogate this pathway, we propose employing single-cell RNA sequencing to resolve cellular heterogeneity and CRISPR-based screens to delineate the functional impact of each molecular component. Moreover, we will explore therapeutic strategies using nanotechnology-driven engineered EVs and miRNA antagonists to specifically disrupt this EV-mediated reprogramming, aiming to restore effective immune surveillance and improve cancer immunotherapy outcomes.
Abstract: We propose that tumor cells secrete extracellular vesicles (EVs) that are biochemically enriched with the oncogenic microRNAs miR-21 and miR-155 together with cytokine modulators such as IL-6 and GM-CSF. Upon uptake by mature myeloid cells—facilitated by this defined pro-inflammatory cytokine milieu—the delivered miRNAs induce targeted downregulation of the transcription factors IRF-8 and C/EBPα, thereby reprogramming myeloid differentiation toward an immunosuppressive, myeloid-derived suppressor cell (MDSC) phenotype. Leveraging advanced technologies including single-cell RNA sequencing and CRISPR-based functional screens, this study aims to dissect the cell-specific molecular dynamics of EV-mediated reprogramming. Furthermore, by developing engineered EVs or miRNA antagonists through modern nanotechnological approaches, we aim to interrupt this EV-miRNA axis to restore normal myeloid differentiation and enhance the efficacy of cancer immunotherapy.
Orignal_vs_New: The revised hypothesis retains the original chain of events—tumor EV secretion, delivery of miR-21 and miR-155, downregulation of IRF-8 and C/EBPα, and MDSC accumulation—but now explicitly defines the cytokine milieu by incorporating cytokines like IL-6 and GM-CSF and clarifies their role in enhancing EV uptake. It integrates contemporary technologies such as single-cell RNA sequencing and CRISPR screens to dissect cell-specific responses and provides a more detailed and practical therapeutic strategy by proposing nanotechnology-based engineered EVs or miRNA antagonists to counteract the EV-miRNA mediated reprogramming. This new formulation directly addresses the critiques regarding mechanistic ambiguities and specificity of the cytokine contribution, thereby enhancing both the scientific rigor and translational potential of the original hypothesis.
